content.title: Identifying Research Questions and Testable Hypotheses
content.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying the core research question or testable hypothesis in an ACT Science passage. A strong hypothesis connects a manipulated variable to a specific, measurable outcome in a way that can be proven true or false through experimentation.
learning_objectives: Identify the manipulated variable and its specific levels or groups.
Identify the specific measurable outcome, including units and time points.
Formulate or recognize a testable hypothesis that compares specific groups on a measurable outcome.

sections.title: The Components of a Testable Hypothesis
sections.content: A testable hypothesis is a specific, falsifiable statement that predicts how a change in one variable affects another. To identify one, you must first isolate the Manipulated Variable (the factor the researcher intentionally changes, such as different concentrations of a solution) and the Measurable Outcome ( the quantifiable response, such as mass in grams or time in seconds). A valid hypothesis must be narrow; vague terms like 'better' or 'healthier' are not testable unless they are defined by a specific metric.

sections.title: The Outcome-Measure Hypothesis Builder
sections.content:
When analyzing an ACT Science experiment, follow these three steps: 1. Name the manipulated variable and its exact levels (e.g., 0%, 5%, and 10% salt concentration). 2. Name the specific measurable outcome and the time point (e.g., average root length after 7 days). 3. Construct a comparative statement (e.g., 'Plants in 5% salt will have shorter average root lengths after 7 days than plants in 0% salt').

![A flow chart showing the steps to identify a testable hypothesis: Identify Manipulated Variable, Identify Measurable Outcome, and Formulate Comparative Statement.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/16ded284-b8af-4a2d-aae9-fd1a72cc9694-1786506611827-185.webp)

sections.title: Falsifiability and Specificity
sections.content: A hypothesis is only useful if it can be tested and potentially disproven. Avoid 'absolute' language like 'always' or 'without exception,' as scientific data usually involves averages and sample variation. Furthermore, ensure the hypothesis stays within the scope of the data provided. If the experiment measures height, the hypothesis should not make claims about DNA or internal chemical changes that were not actually observed.

worked_examples.question:
An experiment involves three groups of 10 seedlings. Group 1 receives no fertilizer, Group 2 receives Fertilizer A weekly, and Group 3 receives Fertilizer B weekly. After 4 weeks, the mean height of each group is recorded in centimeters. Which of the following is a valid testable hypothesis for this study?

A. Fertilizer A makes plants grow better than no fertilizer.
B. Plants given Fertilizer A will have a greater mean height after 4 weeks than plants given no fertilizer.
C. Fertilizer B changes the plant's genetic structure to improve growth.
D. Every plant given Fertilizer A will be taller than every plant given no fertilizer.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the manipulated variable (Fertilizer type: None, A, B). Step 2: Identify the measurable outcome (Mean height in cm after 4 weeks). Step 3: Evaluate the choices. Choice A is too vague ('grow better'). Choice C assumes a mechanism (genetics) not measured in the study. Choice D uses absolute language ('every plant') which is rarely supported by mean data. Choice B is the correct testable hypothesis because it specifies the groups, the exact measurement, the time point, and a directional comparison.

common_mistakes: Choosing a hypothesis that uses vague descriptors like 'healthier' or 'more effective' instead of specific measurements.
Selecting a hypothesis that explains 'why' something happens (internal mechanisms) when the experiment only measures 'what' happens (external outcomes).
Picking 'absolute' statements that claim a result will occur for every single subject rather than focusing on group averages or trends.
exam_tips: Look for the 'if/then' structure or comparative language (e.g., 'greater than', 'less than').
Check the units: A good hypothesis often mentions the specific units (cm, sec, pH) or time frames used in the data tables.
Eliminate choices that discuss variables not mentioned in the passage text or data figures.
content.recap: A testable hypothesis must link a specific manipulated variable to a quantifiable outcome. It should be comparative, directional, and limited to the scope of the measurements provided in the experiment.

knowledge_claims.content: A testable hypothesis is a specific, falsifiable statement predicting the relationship between a manipulated variable and a measurable outcome.
The manipulated variable is the factor intentionally changed by the researcher, such as different types of fertilizer or different temperatures.
The measurable outcome is the quantifiable response recorded during the experiment, such as mass in grams or height in centimeters.
To build a hypothesis, one must identify the specific levels or groups of the manipulated variable and the exact time point of the measurement.
Vague terms like 'better,' 'healthier,' or 'improved' make a hypothesis untestable unless they are tied to a specific metric.
A valid hypothesis must be testable using the data provided in the passage, rather than assuming unmeasured internal mechanisms like DNA changes.
A hypothesis should generally avoid absolute terms like 'always' or 'without exception' because scientific data typically reflects averages and variation.
A testable hypothesis often uses comparative language, such as 'greater than' or 'less than,' to relate two or more experimental groups.
If an experiment measures mean plant height at 4 weeks, the hypothesis should specifically reference 'mean height' and the '4-week' mark.
A research question or hypothesis is only valid if there is a clear way to prove it false (falsifiability) based on experimental results.
Levels of a manipulated variable refer to the specific values or categories used, such as 0 mg, 10 mg, and 20 mg of a drug.
A directional hypothesis predicts the specific nature of a change (e.g., an increase or decrease) rather than just stating a change will occur.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 6: Origins of Bright Crater Rays
Three students discuss why some young impact craters have bright rays extending across the surface.

Student 1: The rays consist mainly of fresh material excavated from beneath a dark, weathered surface. With time, exposure to radiation and tiny impacts darkens the rays until they resemble the surrounding ground.

Student 2: The material is not intrinsically brighter. Impact fragments roughen the surface, and the rough texture reflects sunlight toward the observer at certain angles. As small grains settle, the directional reflection weakens.

Student 3: Both excavation and texture matter. Fresh subsurface material begins brighter than the surface, and rough fragment deposits enhance that contrast. Weathering and settling therefore work together to fade the rays.

A controlled test should change one relevant factor while holding others constant mainly in order to:

options.A: guarantee that the preferred hypothesis is correct.
options.C: ensure that every trial produces exactly the same result.
options.D: make differences in the outcome easier to connect to the changed factor.

items.explanation: Controlling other variables improves the interpretability of treatment differences.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 7: Battery Voltage at Different Temperatures
Students placed identical batteries in temperature-controlled chambers for 30 minutes. They then connected each battery to the same resistor and recorded voltage immediately and after 5 minutes. Each temperature condition used a new battery from the same package.

Which factor was held constant and therefore helped make treatment comparisons meaningful?

options.F: resistor, battery type, and conditioning time
options.J: the conclusion written after the experiment

items.explanation: A controlled factor is kept the same across conditions so differences can be attributed more confidently.
